title: Expectations of a paid RPG maker game

posts.author: VOCALKENNI
posts.body: I was wondering, RPGmakers that are released and commercial, what do people expect from it compared to something that is free? I personally wouldn't purchase a game that has the default tilesets or sprites, because there are so many other games like that. But I was wondering what other people think on the matter as well, any comment is appreciated

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
For me, the two most obvious components are the graphics and the writing.
If a game is free, and I have reason to believe some aspect of it will be enjoyable, I'll push through some degree of subpar English. But as soon as you're charging other people for it, I don't think there's any excuse for the writing to not be proofread, spellchecked, whatever you require to make it correct.
The other part is if I'm paying for a product, I require a minimum quality of graphics. The RTP meets that for me, it's higher quality than some older SNES or Genesis games which I'll still replay and consider to have value.
But I won't pay for something that looks like the dev drew it themselves in Paint. I know there are differing opinions on this, and some folks give credit for the fact that it's not the RTP, or the dev put in that effort...but my mother-in-law put time and effort into the cake she baked the other month, and that thing was nasty and I wouldn't eat it.
If the quality isn't indicative of a professional artist, I won't give money for it.
Then there's all kinds of stuff that would cause me to refund a game, but most of it would cause me to delete a free game, too.

posts.author: Ms Littlefish
posts.body: My expectations for a paid RPG Maker game are the same as any other paid game. It’s written well, it’s fun, it works, it looks good, it sounds good. posts.author: CleanWater
posts.body: Graphics calls attention, of course, but for RPGs what's really matter is the story. If the story is well told, it makes me want to play it until the end. However, it's hard to decide if I should purchase the game or not just by looking at the store page description. That's why I believe developers should provide a demo.

posts.author: ZimXero
posts.body:
A game needs one or more "Amazing" features to warrant being pay to play.  It must have style cohesion and be free from glitches and regular typos or errors.   RTP or vanilla categories are fine as long as they are not sloppy.  After playing, most players must be glad they played it.
Categories that make a game worth the experience include:
Amazing graphics
Amazing story
Amazing combat strategy or experience
Amazing extra events, puzzles, or mechanics that stay fresh and engaging
Amazing ambience - the world feels real and exciting to explore

posts.author: RCXGaming
posts.body:
Here's what I want to see when an RM game has a price tag. The more it costs, the less these are optional.
- Professional art, preferably something that's moved away from the bland medieval / stubby chibi style that you see in the RTP.
- Professional writing. If your game is about story and your writing is worse than a free game, I
will
roast you.
- A solid game loop that isn't just smacking the enemies until they die. Make me use more than 2% of my brain.
- Proper sound design. [y'all know how I feel about this.]
But to really have a stand-out game, you genuinely need these two things:
- Give me new / novel concepts for your game. I flock to the weirdo arthouse RPG Maker games that are often horror because these people are trying to do something different, even if their gameplay isn't there. But (almost) every time someone tries to make an actual RPG in this engine, they stick to the old tired fantasy tropes and it's always exhausting to see that on a store page.
Especially when they list off buzzwords like "Inspired by [classic JRPG]", like dawg. We came here for your game, not a copy of someone else's.
- What
features
makes your game unique? What can we see going forward that'll change how we're meant to play your game versus another person's RPG Maker project? For example, I don't see a lot of RM games take the actual environment where you fight into account - it'd be pretty cool if a game said those did matter.

posts.author: kirbwarrior
posts.body:
For me, it being made in RPG Maker only matters in one very specific regard; RPG Maker games that cost $2 on Steam is about the biggest red flag there is for shovelware.
Aside from that, what matters to me is that you have to pay to own the game, not the engine it was made in. There's likely a long list of things I could come up with, but the one that sticks out to me the most is that if the gameplay loop itself is boring, then I will seek a refund. Even an amazing story won't be enough to propel me through dozens of hours of boring combat (I did that once, pushed myself to finish the story despite the mindless gameplay, never again). I also bring this up because tons of other issues can often be gleaned from marketing (especially when something key about the game is
not
shown) but gameplay feel nearly requires actually playing the game to know.
Note that I'm answering the question of what I'd expect in a paid game, not what would get me to buy the game, since I feel like those are two different questions (and I answers the latter in a different thread about that subject).

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
Stop looking at as "How do make RPG Maker game commercial!?!"
And start framing it as: "How do I make a good game?"
Engine has nothing to do with it other than being the tool used to enable your game making.
In that sense, what I look for in commercial games:
Something unique (but also not too high concept, just call me a Trad Gamer - looking at you Devolver and your weird flipping banana games)
Also, sometimes, something that scratches an itch that hasn't been met in awhile - basically the same of an existing game...BUT MORE (this is usually more franchise related)
Appropriate quality bar for the price, or otherwise a sale.
....waifus....and beefcakes? Hear me out...sexy things sell (Alice knows), and unsexy things don't (Concord knows!)
This is all pretty inactionable, so I'll just wrap up by saying:
Make the game you want, but take time to listen to what other people expect within the genre you are making. See if there are any current gaps in that market; a long dormant franchise or an improvement on genre tropes.

I agree with this, but at the same time people who use RPGmaker are familiar with all of the default assets it gives you, and that can be off-putting if you're trying to sell a game, since it makes it seem like you're "lazy" or just didn't bother putting more work into it. You could have a great story, an amazing idea for a game, but when it has all the default RPGmaker assets, it's going to look like every other RPGmaker game out there.
The RPGmaker engine has a lot of medieval styled assets, and it can definitely have a lot to change about your game if your going to use them. Yes, your game could be set in a medieval world, then those assets would fit well. But I also see a lot of people who use them but are not trying to go for that sort of tone or theme, so it affects how the player is feeling the atmosphere.
Otherwise, if you're changing or using your own assets (ie: sprites, tilesets, adding plugins to change UI, ect) then no, i agree that the engine doesn't necessarily have anything to do with a quality of the game, and it relies on the creator.
So my question isn't exactly based on commercial games as a whole, but specifically RPGmaker games, because it can sometimes be difficult to make a unique RPGmaker game that people would want to buy

I'm making a jump to conclusions here, but I think a lot of people think RPG Maker can't make good games because the default game it deploys is a bad game. Every other engine has the same problem, the difference is RPG Maker attracts people who want to do as little work as possible to make a good game.
RPG Maker doesn't have 3D rendering, advanced lighting, physics, or a whole host of nifty tools that modern engines do. But you don't need any of those things to make a good game. You can make a good game just by having a sprite you can move around a map, the ability to interact, variables/switches, show picture, and show text. If someone can't figure out how to make a game (maybe not a good one) with those basic tools... I don't think that person is a game designer.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Sorry, I only skimmed the comments here.  If someone else already covered what I'm about to say, feel free to ignore.
Graphics
Look, I'll be the first person in any forums on any games to say "graphics don't matter to me", but they still do.  Now, I'm not going to buy a game that's "super realistic" and "super amazing looking", just because it is...  But, I'm also not going to ignore a game that has some very rough and hard to read graphics, either.
With graphics, what I'm typically looking for is "this doesn't look bland".  There are very bland ways to use the RPG Maker RTP.  There really are.  A lot of people do (including myself to an extent... i still very much wish for a return to rounded corners and diagonal walls to spice up map design) very bland stuff with the graphics of RPG Maker.  Blocky square buildings.  Too much clutter.  Bad map design.  Cliche map design choices.
If you have a screenshot of a village and it looks like every other village I've ever seen in every other RPG Maker game or RPG in general... I'm mentally docking your game points on "whether I want to play it or not".
Put a pond in there somewhere or something.  Make it less square.  Have some strange building placement, maybe.  I dunno, something that makes it less generic.  And no, a "fountain in the middle of town" doesn't count as "less generic".  Some actual creativity up front will endear me to your product.
If you have creativity, then I'm more likely to not notice your graphics or care about them.  Because, you know, your game is creative rather than manufactured from a template.
Gameplay Loop
If the primary form of your loop is "combat is deep and engaging!" then I always have to go, "Yeah, I'll bet it's neither of those things and I can break it in 5 minutes".
Most often, this phrase in marketing means "pointless busywork" to me.  It means there's a stagger mechanic, or a mechanic to fill a meter, or manage buffs, or... anything other than "make stuff dead".  I'm old.  I like "make stuff dead".  I don't like, "spend 6 actions to kill a basic enemy".  I don't like, "spend 10 minutes fighting a boss".  I like, "make stuff dead".  I like all the various flavors of "make stuff dead".  By "make stuff dead", I mean, "I like to feel powerful in a video game".
I see too many games promise "deep and engaging combat" and it's just code for "you don't make things dead".
But, I also don't appreciate a lot of other gameplay loops either.  I'm generally looking for something that sounds interesting in terms of gameplay.
As an example, let's use Factorio.  The trailer released ages ago shows you 100% the gameplay loop.  Person mining some ore on the ground by hand.  Camera pans and the person gets into a car and drives over to a small set of miners doing the job for him and putting it on a conveyer belt.  The belt then follows a piece of ore through the factory as it's turned into an end product.  The factory gradually getting more complex and more compact as it travels through it.  Then, we follow a train.  The train makes a loop through what it does and can do (including running over the enemies of the game, and showing the remaining enemies not run over, gunned down by turrets and lasers).  Then, it pans over to a rocket that launches.  That explained the gameplay loop perfectly.  You mine resources, build a factory to change it into something else, but there are enemies that will tear down your factory, and you have to defend it... and you do all this to launch the rocket.  Well, okay, that sounds interesting (or, it did when it was the first automation game I'd ever played).
Gameplay loop shown, quickly explained, it looks interesting.
It would also help if RPG Maker games actually had a gameplay loop.  A good chunk of them actually don't.
Premise/Story
I'm looking for something not "stock standard" if you have a premise or a story as a major draw.
No, that doesn't mean I don't want stories of "BBEG is threatening to destroy the world, go stop them".  I do want that.  I like that.  But, if it's "stock standard", then no thank you.  How do we stop the BBEG?  Gather crystals or a McGuffin?  Eh... probably not, unless your McGuffin stuff is done in some interesting way.
If your twist on the forumla is the interesting part, put that up front and center!  That would draw me in.
Let me put that in some context.
I generally don't like "horror" because it's filled so full of tropes and gore, and it doesn't do much interesting.  But, if you have some monsters in it, I might tune in for the monster.  Unless that monster is overdone.
Now, let's look at "Cabin in the Woods" in terms of movies.  The biggest problem this movie has is that it was never marketed as what its actual twist on the horror genre was.  I put off watching it for YEARS until my friend (who is a massive horror fan) sat me down to watch it.  I was instantly hooked on the movie the moment it reveals "here's how it's not like your typical slasher movie".  The premise is amazing and ranks it among one of my favorite horror films of all time.  But, I also understand why the premise can't be advertised.  The point of the movie is that you're meant to think, "It's just another shlocky horror film" and then it proceeds to deconstruct every trope of the genre.  But, at the same time, if it had been advertised to me as "It's a horror movie deconstruction", I would've popped it into my DVD player automatically because it's promising something interesting to watch.
It's important to get your premise/story out there in a way that differentiates it from all the normal schlock games in the genre.
If you want an RPG Maker game that did this well, take a look at "You Are Not The Hero".  I picked it up on that premise alone.  I did discover I didn't like the game after that fact (not a fan of the gameplay, so it's just "not a Tai" game), but that premise alone drew me into what is actually a pretty cool and interesting game.  It's also funny in places (it got a couple chuckles out of me in the hour and a half I played it, which is more than I can say of most media).  What's the premise?  The hero and his party breaks into your home, steals your stuff, and you set off to get it back (because you're just random NPC Villager who had their home looted for supplies to defeat the BBEG).  Tell me that doesn't at least make you go, "wow, you don't see anything like that very often".
Make the story/premise interesting and I'd be willing to drop some cash on the product. Especially if it remains interesting all through its run time.
Price Tag
Generally, I shy away from $2 RPG Maker games.  Mostly because they seem to be "cash grabs" and "low effort".  If someone is charging $20 for an RPG Maker game, I'll raise my eyebrows, but definitely look over their store page and look for reviews.  The audacity to charge so much means it's either a pretty good scam or it's REALLY worth that cash, and I want to know which it is.
For me, it's about 50/50 on which it is.  But, it's still a good way to pique my interest up front.  Just be prepared for me to be quite angry and seeking a refund if it turns out your $20 price tag is more scam and less quality.
Usually, people will charge what they think they can get away with, without making customers angry.  $2 for a low-effort and low-quality game doesn't usually generate very many bad reviews because "you get what you pay for".  So, I usually ignore anything priced in the "I don't want to make customers angry for low quality games" range.
Now, if you price your game at "free", it's a different circumstance altogether.  It could be that the dev has no idea what their product is worth (no confidence in being able to sell it), or it could be that there's a different monetization option in there (donations, DLC, whatever).  It could even be that the dev is using the game as advertising of quality for their other products.  If it's "free", and seems decently interesting, i'll give it a look.  I want to know why it's priced at $0.  If it's actually really good and fun, then I'm going to see if there's a way to give money or pay for more projects from that developer.  If it's not... then I don't feel bad dropping the game in 30 minutes and leaving a negative review with suggestions on how to do better.

posts.author: Kokoro Hane
posts.body:
I feel like the expectation of a good RM commercial game will vary from person to person, so it all goes down to our personal tastes in the end and what we think is worth the price tag.
For me, story is definitely high on the list. I want to care about the characters. I also would like an interesting world to interact with, whether it is well developed or just teasing me decent lore, as long as something about it is fascinating to me, I'll be happy. Gameplay is also big for me -- it doesn't have to be super fancy or novel, I just want something that feels fun, and isn't either too hard I rage quit early in or so tedious and repetitive I get bored.
I don't mind RTP as long as the graphics are used well. Some people know how to map well with default assets, some will even parallax map with them which makes a huge difference -- even minor edits and recolors can give the RTP a fresh look. But if it is mostly RTP, I do think it should be at a lower price tag. $20 for a mostly RTP game would be pushing it and everything else about it would have to do some heavy lifting to change my mind (which is not impossible). I do think it's nice if we get some original drawn art. Like a good balance of giving an RTP game some unique flair would be maybe some custom insert CGs or the playable characters having uniquely drawn portraits. That I think would make me consider paying a higher price for a game that uses a lot of RTP, but otherwise they should be in a lower price bracket.
Having all original assets of course will be the most eye-catching, but having a pretty game doesn't mean it'll be enjoyable. While all original art would warrant a higher price tag, if the story and gameplay and characters are not interesting, then I'd rather risk paying a high price for an all RTP game where the story and characters and fun gameplay carry it vs. all original assets where that's clearly where all the effort went only.
If a game has voice acting, that would be a super plus for me. I don't think there's enough RM games with voice acting so I won't deny that would grab my attention and tempt me to open my wallet the most. But I am also very, very particular so if actors sound bored or like they're clearly reading from a script, I'd zone out. No matter how good a game is, if the voice acting sucks (and unless there's a special plugin to give it its own sound channel, you can't by default turn off voice over in the options since -- at least with how I use it -- I have to use the sound channel) then it'd kill it. While I love and prefer stellar performances, I actually wouldn't mind really hammy and cheesy performances since at least it has life and is fun and you can laugh at it (so bad it's good) but I dislike mediocre performances and so bad it's bad, it's quite immersion breaking.
Lastly, if a game is paid, I do really appreciate a demo so I can get a taste if it's something I want to buy. Especially if a game is $10 or more. First impressions are everything, so if a demo can convince me I need to play more of this, I'm more likely to buy. Because in the end, regardless if it uses all original assets, a mix of RTP and original, or all out straight out of the box graphics, how it plays and whether or not I care about the story and characters is really what is gonna sell me on the game. (And if it has voice over -- the quality of the voice acting).

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body: I don't differentiate between indie games made in RPG Maker vs any other engine. Generally speaking, the game has to have some unique hook that I can't get from other games. If it's not unique then it has to stand out in some way,  e.g. gameplay, story, etc. Price matters too. The higher the price the higher my expectations will be for production values.

For me, the absolute most important part is the how the game feels to play.
As long as the graphics are decent and work in the context of the game, they are fine to me. Obviously, constant "lazy" use of assets that are not even well used is a red flag etc.

posts.author: hyunko
posts.body: Honestly it is something of a vague answer, but if a game is paid it should really show some honest effort in all areas. A game can have competent custom art assets, but if something such as say the music or writing isn't up the same general level of quality it creates a real nasty juxtaposition. This also holds at a more focused level if the game has say, for example, art assets that clash because they are sourced from different places and there is no consistent direction with all of them.
